sentence: Oh, fantastic, another Monday. Truly the highlight of my week. I was just lying awake at five in the morning thinking, you know what would really brighten my mood? Spreadsheets. A meeting that should have been an email. Three coffee refills before I can form a complete sentence. Naturally, the office printer chose today to die, because of course it did, and obviously the IT ticket I submitted last week is still pending. What a wonderful way to start the day.

Wow, my alarm went off at six. What a thrilling surprise. I had absolutely no idea that would happen, despite setting it myself last night. And of course the coffee maker is broken this morning, because clearly the universe has decided I'm having too much fun already.

Nothing says good morning quite like discovering you're out of milk five minutes before you need to leave. Brilliant planning on my part. Truly inspired. I'll just enjoy this lovely black coffee that tastes like regret and motor oil, and pretend everything is going wonderfully.

Oh good, the traffic is backed up for three miles. I love sitting in my car watching the same brake lights for forty minutes. It's basically a hobby at this point. Definitely the best possible use of my finite time on this earth.

My boss scheduled a seven AM meeting, which is great because I was just thinking how my Monday needed more cheerful interactive group experiences before sunrise. The presentation has forty-two slides. I have never been more excited to be alive.

The weather forecast called for sunshine. Naturally, it is pouring. I'm absolutely shocked. This has never happened before in the history of weather forecasts being wrong. I'll just walk to work in my completely soaked dress shoes and have a wonderful day, thanks for asking.

Oh, my favorite. The shower water is cold again. What a delightful Monday surprise. I was hoping to start the week with the icy embrace of plumbing failure, and lo and behold, the universe has provided. Truly, the gods smile upon me.

I love how my Monday outfit looked perfectly fine in the mirror but the moment I sat down in the car, the coffee stain materialized out of thin air. Magic. Real, actual magic. I'm going to walk into the office looking like a Jackson Pollock painting and pretend it's an intentional fashion statement.

Three emails marked urgent before eight in the morning. Wonderful. Clearly the world was on fire all weekend and only I can put it out. I'm so glad my employer values my time and respects boundaries between work and personal life.

Forgot my badge. Again. The security guard who has seen my face every single weekday for three years now needs me to call HR for a temporary pass. Obviously. That makes complete sense. We've never met, you and I. Total strangers. Better double-check that ID.

Oh wonderful, I've been on hold for forty-seven minutes listening to the same fifteen seconds of smooth jazz. I'm having the time of my life. Truly. The hold music is the highlight of my afternoon. I hope this lasts forever. Just me, my phone, and Kenny G's distant cousin on a permanent loop.

Have you tried turning it off and on again? What a revolutionary idea. I never would have thought of that on my own. Thank goodness for trained professionals. Let me try that profound technical solution right now and report back. I'm sure it will solve everything.

Yes, I'm absolutely certain it's plugged in. I have looked at the outlet eleven times. The little light is on. It's been on for an hour. But please, do walk me through checking it again, because clearly I am the kind of person who calls technical support without checking that basic thing first.

I love how the recording assures me that my call is very important to them. So important. So vital. Just not important enough to actually answer in any reasonable amount of time. My call is important the way a museum artifact is important, behind glass, looked at occasionally, never touched.

Oh fantastic, they're transferring me to a different department. The fourth one today. I'm sure this time they'll actually be able to help me, unlike the previous three departments who all assured me, with great confidence, that I had reached the wrong department.

Of course the call dropped right when I was about to give my account number for the third time. What a stunning coincidence. The phone gods clearly favor me today. I shall now redial and reexplain my entire problem to a completely new representative who has no notes from the previous three calls.

Yes, I'd love to take a brief survey at the end of this call about my experience. I've been thinking of nothing else for the last ninety minutes. I cannot wait to give a rating that accurately reflects my deep, profound satisfaction with this customer service journey.

The chatbot is being so helpful. It just suggested I restart my router. For the seventh time. In a single conversation. Truly the future of customer service is here, and it has the long-term memory of a particularly forgetful goldfish.

Oh, my issue is not covered by my warranty. Of course it isn't. Naturally. That would be too convenient. The warranty covers everything except the specific thing that has gone wrong, which is exactly the situation I had assumed when I purchased it.

What a treat to learn that the technician will arrive sometime between eight in the morning and six in the evening. Such a narrow window. I'll just clear my entire day to accommodate, because obviously my schedule revolves around the cable company's vague approximation of time.

Oh, brilliant, the group project is due tomorrow and Greg has done absolutely nothing. Just as predicted. Truly shocking. I never would have foreseen this. Greg, who has not responded to a single message in the group chat for two weeks, now wants to know if we can summarize his contribution for him.

How wonderful, the professor has assigned us into groups randomly, and I have been paired with the three people who have not attended a single lecture this semester. This will surely be a productive and well-distributed collaborative effort. I cannot wait to do all the work and share the grade equally.

I love when Brittany suggests we should meet up to discuss the project and then cancels every single proposed time citing reasons such as being tired, being not in the mood, and once, memorably, being a Tuesday. Truly an invaluable member of our team.

Wonderful, Devon has finally added his slides to the shared document, twelve hours before the deadline. They are blank. Two blank slides with our names on them in Comic Sans. What a magnificent contribution. I'm sure the professor will be thoroughly impressed by his initiative.

Oh joy, Marcus has decided at the eleventh hour that the entire project should be restructured around his vision, which he has just now thought of, and which contradicts the outline we all agreed on three weeks ago. Naturally. This is fine.

I am so excited that Jenny will be presenting our research. Jenny, who has confused our topic with another group's topic on three separate occasions, including during the rehearsal yesterday. This presentation will go beautifully. I have complete confidence in the outcome.

Of course Chad's section is plagiarized. Why would I have assumed otherwise? Just because we explicitly discussed academic integrity at our first meeting and he nodded vigorously and said he understood. Clearly that nod was binding. Clearly.

Oh wonderful, Stephanie has used eleven different fonts in her portion of the document, and at least three of them appear to be in different languages. The bibliography is in Wingdings. A bold artistic choice. The professor will surely appreciate the avant-garde formatting.

Yes, please, let's have another two hour meeting where we discuss what we will discuss in our next meeting. This is exactly the productive use of everyone's time that I had in mind. We are absolutely going to finish this project ahead of schedule at this rate.

Tyler has just submitted his portion. It is one paragraph long. The assignment is fifteen pages. He has written, in this paragraph, that the topic is complex and warrants further investigation. Brilliant. Pulitzer-worthy. Truly the analysis we have all been waiting for.

Oh, a heatwave. How marvelous. Just what I was hoping for during my outdoor wedding next Saturday. The forecast says one hundred and four degrees. Perfect weather for two hundred guests in formal wear standing on asphalt. I'm sure no one will faint. I have planned for this.

Snow in April. What a treat. I had just put away my winter coat and dug out the sandals. Mother Nature, you absolute comedian, you. The cherry blossoms are now wearing little white hats. Adorable. Truly the seasonal transition I had been dreaming of.

Hurricane warning issued the day before my flight. Of course. Naturally. Why wouldn't there be? I planned this trip six months ago specifically so a major weather system could ruin it. I'm sure the airline will be very accommodating about the rebooking fees.

Eight inches of rain in two hours. Excellent. The basement, which the previous owners assured me had never flooded, is now hosting an indoor swimming event. I'm sure they were being completely honest and not at all selectively interpreting the historical record.

Wonderful, the third polar vortex of the season. I love when my pipes burst. It's like a fun surprise from the plumbing. I get to pay several thousand dollars to a professional and also live without water for four days. Truly the winter experience I signed up for when I moved north.

Oh, a perfectly clear sunny day. On Tuesday. When I'm stuck in the office. The one day this month it isn't raining is the day I cannot enjoy it. The universe really does have a sense of humor, and it is being absolutely hilarious right now.

How fantastic, the forecast called for ten percent chance of rain, and naturally it has been pouring since I left the house without an umbrella. Ten percent. Clearly we are operating in the rare and exotic scenario predicted by that ten percent. I should buy a lottery ticket.

A tornado watch on the day of the picnic. What an absolutely charming addition to the festivities. The kids will love watching the sky turn green while we hide under the gazebo. This will be a memorable family gathering for sure, for entirely the wrong reasons.

Brilliant, an ice storm. Just what the morning commute needed. A bit of light slippage to keep things interesting. I'm sure the three cars currently spinning in slow circles on the overpass are also enjoying this delightful weather event.

Oh good, ninety percent humidity. I love when my hair becomes a separate organism. I love walking five steps and immediately needing a shower. The air today feels like a warm wet blanket, which is exactly the sensory experience I wanted before my outdoor work event.

Oh, fantastic, another celebrity has discovered the miracle cure to weight loss that involves drinking only celery juice and standing on one leg during a full moon. Truly groundbreaking science. I will rush to my local grocery store immediately. The medical establishment has been wrong all along, and we have a former reality television personality to thank for setting them straight.

Yes, I'm sure cutting out an entire macronutrient group will solve everything. Carbs have been the secret villain all along. Bread, the ancient grain that sustained civilizations for ten thousand years, was actually our greatest enemy. How could we have been so blind. Thank goodness for influencers.

The new wellness book says I should be drinking my coffee with butter, salt, and a tablespoon of grass-fed unicorn tears. Naturally. This is clearly more credible than the recommendations of every nutritionist with an actual degree. I will be ordering the unicorn tears off Amazon immediately.

Oh wonderful, the protein shake at the smoothie place costs fourteen dollars and contains a substance that the menu calls activated almonds. Activated. As if they were sitting there, dormant, and someone had to wake them up with a little speech. I am paying for almond enlightenment.

Yes, I'd love a salad. With dressing on the side. And no croutons. And could you substitute the chicken for grilled chicken, which I realize is the same thing but I read it in a magazine. And could the lettuce be massaged. Massaged lettuce is essential. Thanks so much.

Brilliant, intermittent fasting is the new revolutionary discovery, despite human beings having involuntarily intermittently fasted for the entire history of our species before grocery stores. We have rebranded not eating for a while as biohacking. Magnificent. Truly innovative thinking.

Of course this cleanse will detoxify my organs. My liver, an organ specifically designed to detoxify, has obviously been doing a terrible job all these years and needs the help of a forty-dollar bottle of green sludge to function properly. How did I ever survive without this.

I love how the diet book is six hundred pages long and the actual diet plan is essentially eat less and move more, but dressed up in fifteen different chapters about cellular inflammation and ancestral wisdom and quantum metabolism. Worth every penny of the twenty-eight dollars.

Marvelous, the new superfood is a berry from a remote mountain region that only twelve people have heard of, costs forty dollars a pound, and tastes like cardboard soaked in disappointment. But it has antioxidants. So many antioxidants. I will eat them by the handful and live forever.

Naturally, my friend who lost twelve pounds on the new diet thinks it will work for everyone. Because metabolism is not at all influenced by genetics, age, sleep, stress, hormones, or any of the dozens of other variables that vary wildly between human beings. Just buy the book.

Oh wonderful, the self-checkout machine wants me to place my item in the bagging area. I have placed it in the bagging area. I am pressing the item firmly into the bagging area. The machine remains unconvinced. I have now summoned an attendant, who is helping six other people, all of whom are having the exact same problem with their respective machines. Truly the future of retail.

Yes, unexpected item in the bagging area. The unexpected item is the item I just scanned. The item I am attempting to purchase. The expected item, really, if we think about it. But the machine has decided it is unexpected, and so we shall all wait.

Of course the only working self-checkout out of the twelve installed is the one with no card reader. Excellent design. The other eleven machines stand silent, like a row of expensive monuments to corporate cost-cutting. The one cashier on duty has a line of nineteen people.

Brilliant, the machine is now demanding I scan my loyalty card. I do not have a loyalty card. I have never had a loyalty card. I have explained this to the machine in a calm voice for the last ninety seconds. The machine does not care. It blinks at me, expectantly.

Oh fantastic, the produce code lookup feature is somehow more complicated than just typing in the number. I am now scrolling through pictures of mangoes, trying to determine if my mango is a champagne mango or a regular mango or perhaps a Tommy Atkins mango. I just wanted to buy a mango.

Wonderful, an unexpected item alert again. I placed nothing in the bagging area. There is nothing there. The machine is now hallucinating items into existence. We are now in a philosophical dispute with the kiosk about the nature of reality and what exists.

Of course the machine ran out of receipt paper just as my transaction was completing. I will simply trust that I was charged correctly, and that the cash I deposited went into the correct accounting category, and that no one will ever ask me for proof of this purchase.

I love the cheerful chirping noise the machine makes every time it suspects me of stealing. The aggressive friendliness of automated retail is one of life's great pleasures. It feels like being scolded by a sentient kazoo.

Naturally, the machine has now frozen on the payment screen. Completely frozen. My card has been swiped four times. Each swipe was apparently invisible to the kiosk. The attendant has been paged. The attendant is not coming. I have aged visibly during this transaction.

Oh good, the receipt is printing now, all four feet of it, because somehow buying eggs and bread generated a receipt longer than my arm filled with coupons for products I will never purchase. Excellent use of resources.

Oh, our flight has been delayed again. What a treat. The third update from the gate agent in twenty minutes, each one pushing the boarding time back by another fifteen minutes, like a very slow countdown to nothing. We're all just standing here, watching the screen, eating six-dollar pretzels and pretending this is fine.

Of course the delay was caused by weather. There is no weather here. The sun is shining. Birds are singing. But somewhere, in a place none of us have heard of, there is allegedly weather, and so we shall sit here for six additional hours and trust that this is true.

Wonderful, they're offering us food vouchers worth seven dollars at an airport where a small bottle of water costs nine. I shall use this voucher wisely, perhaps to buy a single mint or to fund a portion of a small bag of chips.

Oh fantastic, the gate has been changed. Naturally. The new gate is, of course, at the opposite end of the terminal, which I will need to sprint to with my carry-on bag bouncing against my hip, dodging slow-walking tourists, while clutching the seven-dollar food voucher.

Marvelous, the inbound aircraft has just arrived, which is normally good news, except that it arrived from a city that is famously not the one our crew is coming from. So we are still waiting on a flight crew. Which has not yet been assigned. Excellent communication.

I love how the gate agent's announcement assures us that they are working to get us in the air as quickly as possible. Quickly. The flight was supposed to leave four hours ago. Quickly is a beautiful word that has no relationship to anything happening in this terminal right now.

Oh delightful, we have now been informed that the delay is due to a mechanical issue, which is comforting because I love hearing that the airplane I am about to board has a mechanical issue, and that the issue has been resolved according to a man holding a wrench.

Of course they are now boarding by zone. I am in zone seven. There are six zones. I have been recategorized. I will board last, after the priority passengers, the platinum passengers, the gold passengers, the silver passengers, and the people who paid extra for the privilege of standing in line slightly earlier.

Brilliant, my connecting flight is now also delayed. Which would be wonderful news if it were delayed enough to wait for me, but it has been delayed only twelve minutes, while my current flight has been delayed three hours. The math is not favorable.

Lovely, the gate agent has now informed us that the flight has been canceled entirely. After eight hours of false hope. Eight hours of being told boarding would begin shortly. I have made peace with my fate. I shall live here now, in terminal C, near the soft pretzel kiosk.

Oh, my favorite place. The DMV. I love taking a number that is in the high four hundreds when they are currently serving number fifty-three. I have brought snacks. I have brought a book. I have brought my will, in case I die here.

Of course the form I filled out online does not count and I need to fill out the same form again, on paper, with a pen chained to the desk that does not have ink. Excellent. I will just etch my information into the paper using sheer force of will.

Brilliant, the clerk has now informed me that I needed two forms of identification, not the one I brought, despite the website specifically saying one form would be sufficient. The website is, evidently, decorative. I shall return tomorrow, and the next day, and the day after.

Wonderful, the photo for my new license has been taken. I look like I have just been informed of a death in the family. I am unable to retake it. This will be my official identity for the next ten years. I look like a hostage in the photograph.

Oh fantastic, only one of the fifteen windows is staffed today. The other fourteen clerks have presumably been raptured. The remaining clerk is helping a gentleman whose situation appears to involve four separate vehicles, three jurisdictions, and a possibly forged title from 1987.

Of course the kiosk that prints the numbers is broken. So we are now organizing ourselves by honor system, glaring at each other suspiciously to determine who arrived first. A grandmother and a tattooed man in his thirties are currently in a tense standoff about who entered the building at nine fifteen.

Naturally, the document I brought, certified yesterday by a notary, is not the correct kind of certification. There is a different kind of certification. It is performed by a different person, at a different location, for a different fee. Of course there is.

Wonderful, the credit card machine is down. I will pay in cash, which I do not have, because I assumed that a government office in this century would accept credit cards. I will now walk three blocks to an ATM, lose my place in line, and start the entire process over.

Oh, my number was just called. I missed it because I was in the bathroom for ninety seconds. The clerk is now calling the next number. I am informed that I will need to take a new number and wait again. I have been here for four hours. I am calm. I am calm.

Brilliant, the clerk has informed me that I have, in fact, come to the wrong DMV office. This office handles only commercial licenses. The office I needed is on the other side of town and closes in thirty minutes. The drive takes thirty-five.

Oh, fantastic, another match whose profile is just five photos of him holding fish. Big fish, small fish, medium fish. Not a single sentence in his bio. Just the fish. I'm sure he has a thrilling personality to match the rich variety of aquatic life he has personally vanquished.

Yes, I would love to meet up with a man whose opening message is hey. Just hey. The full message. Such effort. Such verbal craftsmanship. I can already tell our future conversations will be rich with substance and depth.

Of course his profile says he is six foot two. They all say six foot two. There has apparently been some sort of genetic mutation in the dating pool, where ninety-eight percent of men are exactly six foot two and the remaining two percent are six foot three. The bell curve has been outlawed.

How wonderful, a man whose only interests, according to his bio, are travel, dogs, and adventure. Three things no other human has ever enjoyed. Truly a unique individual standing out from the crowd. I'm sure he loves trying new things and is just as happy at a fancy restaurant as he is in jeans and a t-shirt.

Brilliant, the date that seemed promising on the app has just informed me, in person, that he is in an open relationship. Which was not mentioned in his profile. Or in any of the messages we exchanged for two weeks. This is a delightful surprise. I love surprises.

Oh joy, another profile featuring a man cuddling a tiger. Always with the tiger. Always at the same Thailand sanctuary. I am beginning to suspect this is the same tiger, photographed with a rotating cast of bad first dates.

Naturally, he has now ghosted me. After three weeks of daily messages and one extremely promising first date. Just vanished. Like a magic trick. Truly inspired communication skills. I'm sure he is doing wonderfully out there, ghosting other women with the same flair.

Oh fantastic, his profile says he loves to laugh. What a rare and special quality. I had been hoping to find someone who specifically enjoyed the act of laughing, as opposed to all the people out there who hate laughter and avoid it at all costs.

Of course he is allergic to my cat. Mentioned this for the first time three months in. Despite the fact that I have a cat-themed bio, two photos with the cat, and have brought up the cat in approximately forty conversations. Excellent listening skills. Truly attentive.

Wonderful, his last picture was clearly from 2014, judging by the haircut, the phone he was holding, and the now-deceased family pet visible in the corner of the frame. I'm meeting a completely different person tonight, archeologically speaking.

Oh, fantastic, the gym is packed today with people who clearly made New Year's resolutions to occupy every single piece of equipment simultaneously. The squat rack is being used as a place to scroll TikTok. The bench press is being used for casual seated conversation. I shall just wait here patiently and pretend that this is what fitness looks like.

Of course the man on the treadmill next to me is grunting like he is birthing a small woodland creature, despite walking at four miles per hour. The acoustics here are wonderful. Truly a meditative environment for cardiovascular exercise.

Wonderful, someone has draped their towel over the only functioning rowing machine and walked away, presumably to a different planet, since they have not returned in forty-five minutes. The towel has now become a permanent fixture. We have all silently agreed to honor it.

Oh good, the personal trainer is yelling at his client about commitment and discipline at seven in the morning. I'm so glad I paid forty dollars a month to be near this man and his motivational screaming. It really enhances the experience of trying to lift weights quietly in the corner.

Naturally, the only available locker is the one on the very top, requiring an acrobatic maneuver to reach. I shall now climb the bench, balance precariously, and shove my gym bag into a slot that appears to be designed for someone seven feet tall.

Brilliant, the gentleman doing curls has set up shop in the dumbbell rack, blocking access to every weight between ten and forty pounds. He is using two of them. The other forty-eight are decorative. He stares into the mirror with great purpose.

Oh delightful, the woman next to me is taking a phone call on speaker while doing lunges. I'm now privy to her detailed conversation about her sister's divorce. I had been wondering what dramatic real estate disputes were occurring in her family, and now I know.

Of course the water fountain is broken. All three of them. Simultaneously. I shall remain magnificently hydrated by licking the condensation off the air conditioning vents, a creative solution to a problem the gym apparently has no intention of fixing.

Lovely, my favorite gym bro is back, the one who films himself doing every set from four angles and then sits on the equipment reviewing the footage for ten minutes between reps. Truly the equipment exists for his cinematographic purposes, not for the rest of us peasants.

Oh fantastic, someone has left a puddle of sweat the size of a small lake on the bench press and walked away without wiping it down. What a generous donation. I'm sure the next person to use this bench will be deeply touched by the gift of bodily fluids left behind.

Oh wonderful, my aunt has just posted another twelve-paragraph status update about her ongoing feud with her neighbor over a fence line that was settled twelve years ago. I cannot wait to read all twelve paragraphs and react with the appropriate emoji combination of crying laughing, prayer hands, and angry red face.

Of course someone in the comments has typed do your research, the universal phrase indicating that they have done no research and would like you to confirm their unsupported beliefs by also doing no research. I shall comply immediately.

Brilliant, the influencer is now apologizing for a thing she said in 2017, in a thirty-minute video filmed in front of a ring light, while wearing a perfectly coordinated outfit, with tears welling up at carefully timed intervals. So spontaneous. So heartfelt. So obviously not rehearsed at all.

Oh good, an old friend from high school has just sent me a long message about a once-in-a-lifetime business opportunity. I am thrilled to be remembered. Not because of any genuine connection, but because I have skin that requires moisturizing and apparently she sells the moisturizer.

Naturally, two people who I assumed were friends have now publicly unfriended each other and are subtweeting one another in cryptic posts about energy and growth and removing toxic people from one's life. Truly the high road. So very mature.

Wonderful, the comment section of this perfectly innocuous baking video has somehow devolved into an argument about geopolitics, with three separate users claiming the baker is personally responsible for the decline of Western civilization. All over a banana bread recipe.

Oh fantastic, my cousin has discovered conspiracy theories and is now sharing them at a rate of approximately one per hour, complete with screenshots from a YouTube channel called something like Truth Patriot Awakening 1776. I'm sure each one is more well-researched than the last.

Of course the celebrity has now issued a non-apology apology, in which she is sorry that you were offended, rather than sorry for the thing she did. A masterclass in linguistic deflection. The PR team has earned their fee this week.

Lovely, a strange man on the internet has decided to inform me that I am wrong about a topic I literally have a degree in, and he has done so with the absolute confidence of someone who spent twenty minutes reading the Wikipedia article. I am humbled by his expertise.

Oh delightful, the influencer is now selling a course on how to be authentic. Six hundred dollars. The course materials include her telling other people how to be themselves. The irony has reached such density that it may have collapsed into a black hole.

Oh wonderful, the instructions consist of fourteen pages of pictograms with no words, and one of the pictograms appears to be a tiny man crying next to a screwdriver. Helpful. I now understand precisely how to assemble this bookshelf, by becoming the tiny crying man.

Of course there are extra screws left over. Three of them. The instructions clearly used all of them. But here they are, in my hand, extra. I shall toss them into the kitchen drawer with all the other extra screws from previous assemblies, where they will live forever, screwing nothing.

Brilliant, the wooden dowel I just hammered into the back panel was the wrong dowel, and now I need to extract it without damaging anything. Which is impossible. The dowel and the panel are now married. They will remain married until one of them dies.

Wonderful, the assembly time on the box was listed as forty-five minutes. I have been doing this for three hours. I am at step seven of forty-two. At this rate, I will finish this bookshelf in approximately the year 2031. My children will inherit it.

Oh fantastic, the Allen key included is too small for the screws also included. The Allen key is for some other piece of furniture, presumably one that exists in an alternate dimension. I shall now drive thirty miles to a hardware store, on a Sunday, to purchase the correct size.

Of course I have assembled the entire base of the dresser backwards. The grain is now facing the wall. I noticed this at step twenty-eight, after attaching seventeen screws. The disassembly process will be lovely. Truly the highlight of my Saturday.

Naturally, one of the panels arrived with a giant crack down the middle. The box, of course, was undamaged. The damage occurred entirely inside the sealed packaging. Apparently the wood spontaneously decided to crack in solidarity with my mounting frustration.

Lovely, I have now stepped on three of the small wooden pegs, two of the cam locks, and one screw with my bare foot. The floor is a minefield. The pain is exquisite. Truly a meditation on suffering and home improvement.

Oh good, the drawer doesn't slide properly. It catches on something invisible halfway through. The drawer is sentient and has chosen to resist its purpose. I am willing to negotiate, but the drawer remains firm in its opposition to performing the basic function for which it was designed.

Brilliant, my partner has wandered in to ask how it's going, just at the moment when I am red-faced, sweating, surrounded by tools, and contemplating burning down the apartment. I assured them everything is going great. We are not on speaking terms now.

Oh, what a treat, the venue is now informing me, six weeks before the wedding, that the gazebo I specifically booked is not available because they double-booked it. They are so sorry for the inconvenience. I'm sure my five hundred guests will be thrilled to stand in an open field instead.

Wonderful, the florist has just informed me that the peonies I selected for the bouquet are not in season, despite the fact that I selected them six months ago and was told they would be in season. I shall now choose between hydrangeas and despair.

Of course my mother-in-law has now added eleven more guests to the list without consulting anyone, four of whom we have never met. She insists they are family friends. The venue capacity has been exceeded. The catering deposit was already paid. But please, do continue inviting strangers.

Brilliant, the dress has come back from alterations and is now somehow tighter than the original, despite being explicitly altered for a looser fit. The seamstress assures me this is normal. I'm sure she has never heard the words I asked for the opposite of this.

Oh fantastic, the photographer has just texted to mention that he might be late because of a prior commitment, on the morning of the wedding. He is so sorry. He is the photographer for our wedding. He is texting now. I cannot fathom what prior commitment supersedes this one.

Of course the DJ has just sent us his playlist and it includes seventeen songs that we explicitly marked as do-not-play. The songs are all on the list, helpfully marked with little stars. We discussed this twice. I shall enjoy the Chicken Dance at my elegant evening reception.

Naturally, the bridesmaid dresses have arrived in colors that bear absolutely no resemblance to the sage green I selected. They are a sort of swampy yellow-brown. The vendor insists this is the correct color. I have begun to question the very nature of vision itself.

Wonderful, the caterer is now asking, three days before the event, whether we want chicken or fish, despite our having made this decision four months ago and confirmed it in writing twice. The records have apparently been lost. The catering will surprise everyone, including us.

Oh delightful, my future father-in-law has informed me he will be giving a speech at the reception. He has also informed me that he will not be sharing the contents of this speech in advance. What could possibly go wrong. I am calm. I am calm.

Of course the cake has arrived two hours late, and the topper has fallen off in transit, and one tier is visibly leaning at an angle that suggests imminent collapse. The baker is taking photos. For her portfolio. This is the wedding day. Truly an honor to be part of her artistic journey.

Oh, fantastic, another grocery store sheet cake in the break room. Vanilla, with vanilla frosting, and a faint smear of frosting where someone tried to spell out a name in icing and gave up halfway through. I shall pretend this is festive and consume my mandatory slice while making small talk with Linda from accounts payable.

Of course the birthday card has been circulating for two weeks and the actual recipient has somehow not noticed, despite it being passed openly across desks and signed in front of them by colleagues whispering loudly. The element of surprise is alive and well in this office.

Wonderful, we are now singing the birthday song, slightly off-key, at three in the afternoon, in the fluorescent-lit kitchenette, while clutching paper plates. The birthday person looks like they want to die. I, too, want to die. We are connected in this moment.

Oh good, the same email chain about the same monthly birthday celebration has gone out for the seventh time this year, complete with reply-all responses confirming attendance from people who clearly thought reply-all was the right choice. My inbox is now thrilling.

Brilliant, Greg has brought his guitar to the office birthday party. Greg has not been asked to bring a guitar. Greg is now tuning the guitar. We are all going to listen to Greg play an acoustic version of a popular song, slightly slower and sadder than the original.

Of course Sandra from HR has organized a balloon arch in the conference room, complete with little number-shaped balloons spelling out an age the birthday person has explicitly asked not to be mentioned. Such attention to detail. So personal. So thoughtful.

Lovely, the office birthday card features a handwritten message from Bob that simply reads happy birthday and a signature, in a card that ten other people wrote heartfelt paragraphs in. Thanks, Bob. Your contribution will not be forgotten.

Oh fantastic, the cake has been cut by Karen, who has somehow managed to give herself the largest piece, the corner with all the frosting roses, while the birthday person received a sliver that contains no decoration whatsoever. Truly equitable distribution.

Naturally, the singing is now being recorded by Janet, who has informed everyone she will be sharing the video on the company intranet. The birthday person, mid-bite of cake, will live on in corporate communications history with a grimace forever frozen in time.

Oh delightful, the office party has stretched on for ninety minutes because no one wants to be the first to leave, in case it seems impolite. We are all trapped here, eating warm slices of cake, talking about the weather, until someone, please, anyone, will break the spell.

Oh wonderful, the fitness app has just informed me that I am behind on my daily step goal, despite the fact that I have been walking for two hours. The phone, which lives in my pocket, has apparently been napping. I shall now jog in place for ten minutes to convince it that I am, in fact, alive.

Of course the app is now demanding I share my data with seventeen third-party services in order to access the basic workout I paid for last month. Such a fair exchange. My personal health metrics for a video of a woman doing lunges. Very reasonable.

Brilliant, the gamified rewards system has informed me that I have unlocked a virtual badge for completing three workouts this week. A badge. On a screen. That no one will ever see. I have never felt more accomplished. My life has true meaning now.

Oh good, the app's cheerful voice is now congratulating me on my pace, which is approximately the pace at which a tortoise might amble across a parking lot. I love being condescended to by an algorithm at six in the morning. Truly motivational.

Of course the app has decided to start playing motivational quotes in the middle of my run, completely interrupting my podcast. The quotes are attributed to people who definitely did not say them. I'm sure Aristotle was very passionate about cardiovascular fitness.

Wonderful, the app has flagged that I missed yesterday's workout and is now suggesting I do double today, which is somehow a real recommendation from a real product designed by real human beings. I am sure my body will respond beautifully to this brilliant strategy.

Oh fantastic, the app has now logged a forty-five-minute workout as a quote unquote light activity, despite the fact that I sweated through three layers of clothing and briefly contemplated my own mortality. Light. So very light. Practically a stroll.

Of course the premium upgrade is required to access the feature that simply tells me how far I have run. This is a basic function. The free version gives me access to inspirational quotes and a weekly newsletter. The premium version is required to display a number that the phone has already calculated.

Naturally, the app has crashed mid-workout and lost all my data, including the personal record I just set. I have screenshots of the in-progress display, but the app does not accept screenshots as evidence. The record never existed. The workout never happened.

Oh delightful, the app is now notifying me that my heart rate seems elevated during this resting period. I am, in fact, running. I have been running for twenty minutes. The app cannot tell the difference. I should perhaps be concerned that my fitness tracker cannot identify fitness.

Oh wonderful, the train is delayed again. Naturally. I am so glad I left an hour early for my meeting, because the transit authority has clearly decided that this would be a fantastic day to experience signal problems. The announcer assures us the delay will be approximately ten minutes, which in transit time means thirty-five minutes.

Of course the only available seat on this packed bus is next to the gentleman who is loudly eating a tuna sandwich. The aroma fills the entire vehicle. Other passengers are now visibly leaning away. I have made my choice. I will stand.

Brilliant, the bus has just driven past my stop, despite my pulling the request cord twice and standing visibly at the door. The driver has not noticed. I will now ride this bus to a neighborhood I have never been to and find my way back.

Oh fantastic, someone has decided to play music from their phone on speaker, with no headphones, at full volume. The choice is a remix of a popular song that has been auto-tuned beyond recognition. The other passengers and I are now bonded by shared misery.

Of course the train doors closed in my face exactly as I reached the platform. The conductor made eye contact with me, smiled, and pressed the button. We have entered a new dimension of customer service, one where the staff actively prevent customers from receiving service.

Wonderful, the air conditioning in this subway car is broken, in August, during a heat wave. We are all sweating gently into each other's shoulders. The smell is incredible. Truly the public transit experience the city brochures promised.

Naturally, the elevator at the station is out of service, which is fantastic news for the woman with the stroller, the man in the wheelchair, and the elderly couple with luggage. I'm sure they will appreciate the four flights of stairs as a fun urban adventure.

Oh good, the fare collection machine is now refusing to accept any payment method, including the contactless tap that worked yesterday. A line is forming behind me. I am gesturing at the machine. The machine is unmoved by my gestures. We are at an impasse.

Brilliant, the train has just stopped mysteriously between stations, the lights are flickering, and the announcer is delivering an unintelligible message that sounds like it might be either we apologize for the delay or there is a small fire. Either way, we are all calm.

Lovely, the man across from me on the train is clipping his fingernails. In public. On the train. With great deliberation. The little crescents of nail are flying in various directions. I will treasure this memory for the rest of my life.

Oh fantastic, the smart bulb has decided to update its firmware at three in the morning, turning itself on at full brightness in my bedroom. The app assures me this is a wonderful feature for keeping devices current. I shall now go shopping for blackout curtains and a return label.

Of course the smart thermostat has decided that 78 degrees in the bedroom is the optimal sleeping temperature, based on its mysterious algorithm. I have changed it manually seventeen times. It changes it back. We are in a relationship now. Neither of us is happy.

Brilliant, the voice assistant has misheard me again and is now playing whale sounds at maximum volume in the living room. I asked it to turn off the lights. There is no apparent connection between my request and its response. The whales sing on.

Wonderful, the smart doorbell has just sent me an alert that there is motion at my front door. The motion is a leaf. A single leaf, blowing in the wind. I have received approximately four hundred such alerts today. The technology is truly transforming our lives.

Oh good, the smart refrigerator is informing me that the milk is expired. I am holding the milk. The expiration date is in two weeks. The fridge insists otherwise. I am not sure how to argue with a fridge. The fridge has more confidence than I do.

Naturally, the smart lock has decided that my correct passcode is no longer correct. It is the same passcode I have used for two years. The lock is now requesting biometric verification, which it does not support. We are locked out of our own house. Excellent design.

Of course the smart vacuum has wedged itself under the couch and is now sending distress signals to my phone. I will have to crawl on the floor to retrieve it, then place it back in its little dock, where it will wait patiently for the next opportunity to wedge itself under the couch.

Oh fantastic, the smart speaker has just spontaneously started laughing in the middle of the night. No one said anything. No one was speaking. The speaker laughed. I have unplugged it. I will not be plugging it back in.

Brilliant, the smart oven now requires me to connect to wifi in order to preheat. Preheating, a feature that has worked on dumb ovens for one hundred years, now requires a software update. The update will take forty minutes. Dinner will be late.

Lovely, my smart watch has just informed me that I should take a deep breath because my stress levels are elevated. The reason my stress levels are elevated is that the smart watch keeps sending me alerts about my stress levels. The irony is not lost on either of us.

Oh wonderful, the teacher is now informing me, fifteen minutes into our scheduled twelve-minute slot, that my child has been struggling with reading for the entire semester. This is the first I am hearing of it. There were three opportunities to mention this earlier, but evidently we are doing the dramatic reveal now.

Of course the other parents have brought baked goods. Homemade. With little decorative flags. I have brought myself, in a sweatshirt that I think might have toothpaste on it. The teacher is comparing me unfavorably to Mrs. Henderson, who I have never met but apparently runs a small bakery.

Brilliant, the teacher has just used the phrase your child is very creative, which I have learned over the years is parent-teacher code for your child does not follow directions and we are concerned. I shall nod gravely and pretend I do not know this.

Wonderful, the conference is being held in a tiny chair clearly designed for someone three feet tall. I am five foot nine. My knees are at my ears. The teacher is comfortable. This is some kind of psychological assessment. I am failing it.

Oh fantastic, the teacher is now showing me a worksheet on which my child has drawn a small purple dragon eating the math problems. The teacher describes this as concerning. I, personally, find it charming. We are not going to agree about this child.

Of course the parent ahead of me in line has decided to use her conference slot to discuss her child's social life in great detail, ten minutes past her allotted time. The teacher cannot escape. We all listen, helplessly, to whether Madison is being included at recess.

Naturally, the teacher has handed me a packet of resources for working on phonics at home, in addition to a packet on math fluency, a packet on social emotional development, and a packet on screen time guidelines. I now have homework. I did not sign up for homework.

Wonderful, the teacher has just said your child marches to the beat of his own drum, which is a beautiful way of saying he will not stop loudly humming during quiet reading time, despite repeated requests. I appreciate the diplomatic framing.

Oh good, the conference has now ended exactly thirty seconds before I was going to ask the one question I actually came here to ask. The teacher is now greeting the next family. I shall save my question for the email thread that will receive an auto-reply.

Brilliant, my child has just received an outstanding effort certificate, which is a delightful way of acknowledging that the actual performance was not outstanding but that the trying was admirable. We shall display this proudly on the fridge, alongside the others.

Oh wonderful, the new office layout has removed all walls, all dividers, and most of the carpeting, so that the sound of every keyboard, every phone call, and every distant sneeze travels freely throughout the entire space. Truly the apex of collaborative design.

Of course the silent floor policy is being enforced by Janet, who silently glares at anyone who clears their throat. Greg, three desks over, has been having a loud phone call about his divorce for the last forty minutes. Janet says nothing. She has chosen her battles.

Brilliant, the hot-desking system means I have no permanent desk and must arrive early to claim one of the better spots, near the window. The good spots are reserved exclusively for senior leadership through a system that is officially first-come-first-served but in practice is not.

Wonderful, the so-called focus pods, the small enclosed booths designed for concentrated work, are all booked solid through the end of next month. Apparently everyone needs to focus. There are six of them. There are three hundred employees. Excellent math.

Oh fantastic, my desk is now positioned directly under an air conditioning vent that blasts cold air on my head for eight hours a day. I have brought a scarf. I am wearing the scarf indoors. My coworkers think this is a fashion choice. It is not a fashion choice.

Of course the sales team has been seated next to the engineering team, despite the fact that the sales team conducts phone calls all day and the engineering team requires absolute silence to function. Truly inspired space planning. The synergy is palpable.

Naturally, the man across from me has chosen to take all his calls on speakerphone, leaning back in his chair, talking loudly about quarterly projections. I am wearing noise-canceling headphones at full volume and I can still hear him. He is louder than my headphones can cancel.

Wonderful, the company has now added a relaxation area in the corner, complete with bean bag chairs and a foosball table. No one uses it. Standing visibly at the relaxation area is considered an admission that one is not working. The bean bags are pristine. The foosball table gathers dust.

Oh good, the new printer is located halfway across the office, requiring a walk past sixteen colleagues to retrieve any printed document. By the time I reach the printer, three other people have collected my documents, returned them to the wrong pile, and walked away.

Brilliant, the smell of someone's microwaved fish has now permeated the entire floor. We are all simultaneously aware of, and powerless to address, the situation. The fish-eater is unfazed. The rest of us breathe through our sleeves.

Oh fantastic, my upstairs neighbor has chosen three in the morning to begin rearranging what appears to be a complete collection of bowling balls. The thuds are rhythmic, almost musical. I am being lulled to sleep by an avant-garde performance art piece I did not consent to attend.

Of course the neighbor's dog has been barking at the same fixed point in the yard for ninety minutes. The neighbor is not home. The dog is alone. The barking is unceasing. I am sure this is exactly the urban living experience I signed a year-long lease for.

Brilliant, the neighbor has now parked their truck across two spaces, blocking my driveway entirely. They have been doing this for three weeks. They have explained that they need the extra room. The HOA has been informed. The HOA is on vacation.

Wonderful, the neighbor's leaf blower is now in operation, at seven in the morning, on a Saturday. The leaves are being blown into a small pile, which the wind will scatter again within the hour. This is a Sisyphean performance and we are all the audience.

Oh good, the neighbor has now sent a passive-aggressive note about the dimensions of my garbage can, which is approximately one inch over the line on his side. He has measured. With a ruler. The note is three paragraphs long. The relationship is, of course, only deepening.

Of course the neighbor is now hosting a backyard party with karaoke, which began at eight in the evening and shows no signs of ending. The selection of songs is curious. We are now on the third rendition of Sweet Caroline. The performer has not improved with practice.

Naturally, the neighbor's tree has shed all of its leaves into my yard, and only my yard, despite the fact that the tree is equidistant between our properties. The leaves have somehow chosen sides. I shall now rake them while the neighbor sips coffee on the porch.

Wonderful, the new neighbor has decided to introduce themselves by complaining about my front porch decorations within ninety seconds of meeting me. The seasonal pumpkin is too large. The wreath is too colorful. We are getting off to such a delightful start.

Oh fantastic, the neighbor is now installing what appears to be a flood light pointed directly at my bedroom window. He has informed me that it is for security. The light is on a motion sensor that triggers whenever a cat walks within thirty feet. I shall be sleeping with a blackout mask.

Brilliant, the neighbor has reported me to code enforcement for the height of my fence, which has been the same height since before he moved in three years ago. I admire his attention to detail. I admire his commitment to making my life slightly worse.

Oh wonderful, the package has been marked as delivered, despite the fact that I am standing on my porch and there is no package. The photo on the delivery confirmation appears to be of someone else's porch. Truly impressive geographic precision from the delivery service.

Of course the courier has now hurled the package containing my new ceramic dishes over the fence, where it has landed in the bushes with a tremendous crash. The shipping label reads handle with care and fragile in three languages. He has handled it with care, indeed.

Brilliant, the delivery has been rescheduled four times now, with the latest notification simply stating that an exception has occurred. The exception is unspecified. The package has not moved from the warehouse for three weeks. I have begun to suspect it does not exist.

Wonderful, the package has been left on the wrong side of the building, behind a dumpster, in the rain. I am now standing in a puddle, retrieving my soggy box, while a stray cat watches me judgmentally from atop the dumpster. A perfect Tuesday afternoon.

Oh fantastic, the delivery driver has rung the doorbell, dropped the package, and bolted before I could answer the door, as if the package were on fire. I now have to chase him down the street to ask about the second package I am also expecting.

Of course the package has been returned to sender, with no explanation, despite the address being printed in large clear letters on the box. The seller charges a restocking fee. I have not received the item. I am paying twice for the privilege of not receiving the thing I paid for.

Naturally, the courier has now placed the package directly in front of the door, blocking it entirely, so that opening the door requires nudging the package across the porch like a curling stone. Excellent placement. I shall now slide my way to freedom.

Wonderful, the tracking number is now saying the package is out for delivery, has been out for delivery for three consecutive days, but somehow remains both out for delivery and not delivered. The package exists in a state of perpetual delivery. Schrodinger's parcel.

Oh good, the package has arrived at last, after only nineteen days of expedited shipping. The expedited shipping cost me an additional twenty dollars. The standard shipping was advertised as taking three to five days. The math here is excellent.

Brilliant, the package has been damaged in transit, the contents are partially crushed, and the box has clearly been opened and re-taped. The label assures me my items have been packed with great care. Someone packed these with great care, and someone else absolutely destroyed them.

Oh, wonderful, the receptionist has confirmed my appointment is at three, despite my having received four text messages and two emails confirming an appointment at four. The receptionist insists the appointment was always at three. I have arrived an hour late for an appointment that does not match the time of my appointment.

Of course the doctor is running ninety minutes behind schedule, which I learned upon arriving at my scheduled time. The waiting room is full of similarly frustrated people, all of whom were also told to arrive promptly. We are bonded by mutual betrayal.

Brilliant, the doctor has now spent four of the seven minutes of my appointment looking at her computer, not at me. The other three minutes consisted of her asking me to repeat information I had already provided in the intake form. Truly personalized medicine.

Wonderful, the nurse has just informed me that I should drink more water. I have explained that I have been hospitalized twice this year for hyponatremia from excessive water intake. The advice remains: drink more water. I shall, I suppose, drink more water.

Oh fantastic, the prescription has not been called in to the pharmacy, despite the doctor's explicit promise that it would be done within the hour. The pharmacy has no record of the prescription. The doctor's office is now closed. I shall enjoy a weekend without my medication.

Of course the bill has arrived, and it is fourteen hundred dollars for what was billed as a routine annual physical. The line items include things called procedures that consisted of the doctor making eye contact and saying how are you feeling. Truly an expensive social interaction.

Naturally, the office has now sent me to a specialist, who has a six-month waiting list, despite the symptoms being described as urgent. I shall simply wait six months to learn whether my urgent symptoms are, in fact, urgent. I'm sure it'll keep.

Wonderful, the patient portal has informed me that my test results are in. I cannot view the results because the system requires a verification code that was sent to an email address I no longer have access to. The results sit, just out of reach, behind a wall of bureaucratic incompetence.

Oh delightful, the office has now informed me that my insurance does not cover the procedure that was previously confirmed as covered. The confirmation was apparently verbal. There is no record. I shall pay out of pocket for a service I was assured would be free.

Brilliant, the medical assistant has now weighed me on a scale that is positioned in the hallway, in full view of three other patients and a passing courier. Privacy is, evidently, optional. My weight is now known to a stranger who is delivering linens.

Oh wonderful, my mother-in-law has arrived three hours early for the weekend visit, while I am still in pajamas and have not yet cleaned the bathroom. She has brought her own pillow. And her own coffee. And a list of comments about the state of the house, ranked by severity.

Of course my father-in-law has spent the first hour of his visit explaining how my front porch railing is poorly constructed. He has not built a railing in his life. He has, however, watched many videos about railings. He is now an expert. The railing remains, defiantly upright.

Brilliant, my mother-in-law has now rearranged my kitchen, ostensibly to help. Nothing is where I left it. The spices are now in alphabetical order, except for the ones she does not approve of, which have disappeared entirely. I shall now spend three weeks finding things.

Wonderful, my in-laws have brought their dog, a small yappy creature, despite our explicit request that they leave the dog at home. The dog has urinated on three pieces of furniture in the first day. The in-laws find this charming. I have begun to lose my will to live.

Oh fantastic, the in-laws have brought a thirty-page itinerary for what was supposed to be a relaxing weekend visit. Each meal is scheduled. Each activity is pre-planned. There is a section labeled spontaneous family bonding from two to four PM on Saturday.

Of course my mother-in-law has now asked me, in the middle of dinner with witnesses, when we plan to have children. She has asked this seven times this visit. The answer remains the same. The question, evidently, has not heard the answer.

Naturally, my father-in-law has decided this is the right moment to share his political views, loudly, over coffee, with my friend who he just met. I had been hoping for an awkward family dinner, and the universe has provided beyond my wildest dreams.

Wonderful, my mother-in-law has now commented on my cooking, suggesting that it would be better if I made it the way her mother used to make it. Her mother died in 1987. I never met her. The recipe is, mysteriously, unavailable. I have failed against an unwinnable benchmark.

Oh good, the in-laws have extended their visit by three days. They had originally planned to leave Sunday. They are now leaving Wednesday. They have not asked. They have simply announced. I shall now cancel my plans, my work, and my mental health, accordingly.

Brilliant, the in-laws have left, finally, but only after my mother-in-law completed a tour of the house pointing out everything that needs fixing, repainting, or replacing. The list is on the fridge. It is four pages. She will be following up by email.

Oh, fantastic, my weekend, which I had set aside for relaxation and personal growth, has now been entirely consumed by laundry, dishes, and the discovery that the bathroom drain has clogged for the third time this month. Truly the rejuvenating two days I was promised by motivational posters.

Of course the dryer has decided to stop drying. The clothes are now spinning in warm circles, technically tumbling but achieving nothing. I shall hang my towels around the apartment like flags of surrender and pretend this is what bohemian living looks like.

Brilliant, I have just discovered that mopping the floor requires moving every piece of furniture in the room. Tasks I had assumed would take twenty minutes will now take three hours. The dust bunnies under the couch have evolved into rabbits, which have started small civilizations.

Wonderful, the vacuum has spontaneously stopped working mid-vacuum, with half the rug clean and the other half still covered in cat hair. I shall just live in this house of two halves, the clean half and the unclean half, separated by an invisible line of failure.

Oh fantastic, the gutters have filled with leaves and now resemble decorative planters. The water is pouring over the side instead of through the downspout. I shall now climb a ladder, in light rain, to dig out three pounds of decomposing organic matter with my bare hands. A perfect Saturday.

Of course I have just discovered an unidentifiable container in the back of the fridge. The contents are gray. The lid is bulging. I do not remember purchasing it. I do not recognize what it once was. I shall throw it out, container and all, and never speak of this again.

Naturally, the lightbulb in the hallway has burned out and replacing it requires a specific size that I do not have. The store is closed. I shall be navigating my home by flashlight tonight. Truly the modern adventure I had been craving.

Wonderful, the lawn mower has died, again, halfway through the lawn. The lawn is now half mowed, with a visible jagged line where one length of grass meets another. It looks like a bad haircut on a giant. I shall now drag the lawn mower to the repair shop.

Oh good, the toilet is making a sound that I would describe as ominous. A sort of gurgling, intermittent, like it is digesting something. I do not want to investigate. I shall pretend I did not hear it, and hope that the sound will resolve itself by Monday.

Brilliant, the dishwasher has now started making a grinding noise and emitting smoke. The user manual suggests this is normal during the first wash. I am on wash number two thousand. The manual is, perhaps, slightly out of date. I shall now wash dishes by hand, like a peasant.

Oh wonderful, this piece consists of a single banana taped to a wall. It is selling for one hundred and twenty thousand dollars. Truly profound commentary on the commodification of art. I shall stand here in the gallery and contemplate the depth of the banana for forty minutes, as is expected of a sophisticated person.

Of course this installation is just an empty room with a single fluorescent bulb humming overhead. The artist's statement is fourteen pages long and uses the word liminality eleven times. I am now in deep dialogue with the void, apparently. The void is silent on the matter.

Brilliant, the painting is a solid red canvas, eight feet by eight feet, titled Untitled Number Seventy-Three. The placard explains that the artist is exploring the boundaries of color and form. He is exploring red. He has chosen red. That is the work.

Wonderful, the sculpture is a pile of trash arranged on the floor. I am told the arrangement is deliberate. I am told the trash is intentional. I am told that this comments on our relationship with refuse. I am also told not to step on the art, which appears identical to the actual trash in the corner.

Oh fantastic, the performance piece is a man sitting silently on a chair for eight hours. He is staring at the wall. The audience members are encouraged to sit across from him and engage in a profound silent communion. I have engaged. I am now profoundly bored.

Of course the photograph is just a blurry image of a streetlight, taken from inside a moving vehicle. The print is selling for three thousand dollars. The artist statement explains that this is an exploration of motion and ephemerality. My phone takes accidental photos like this hourly.

Naturally, the video piece is a forty-three-minute loop of someone slowly peeling an orange. There is no sound. There is no commentary. There is only the orange. I have watched seven minutes. I have aged. I will be different when I leave this gallery.

Wonderful, the artist has glued a thousand cigarette butts to a wooden panel and titled it Smoking Kills. The depth of meaning here, the layers of subtlety, the rich symbolic vocabulary. I shall take many photos and pretend to be moved. The collector's edition prints are available in the gift shop.

Oh delightful, this exhibit requires the viewer to wear a special blindfold while listening to whale sounds, while the actual art is described to them by a docent. The art itself remains unseen. We are experiencing the art conceptually. The actual art may not exist. The whale sounds are real, at least.

Brilliant, the gallery has installed a piece that is just a microwave with a brick inside it. The microwave is running. The brick is not heating up, because it is a brick. The artist's intention, per the wall card, is to challenge our assumptions about utility. Mission accomplished.

Oh wonderful, the yoga instructor is now telling us to honor whatever our body needs in this moment, but is simultaneously demonstrating a pose that would require the flexibility of a contortionist. My body needs to be on the couch. I am dishonoring my body.

Of course the woman next to me is in full splits, balancing on one finger, while I am still attempting to figure out which direction my left foot is supposed to be facing. Truly a beginner-friendly class. Truly inclusive.

Brilliant, the instructor has now decided this is the perfect time for fifteen minutes of pigeon pose, which is a position that consists of folding the body into a shape it was never meant to inhabit, while pretending to feel released and centered. I feel only pain and existential confusion.

Wonderful, the studio is now playing whale sounds layered over a sitar, while a smoke machine produces lavender-scented fog. I am being aggressively relaxed against my will. The atmosphere is being applied to my forehead with all the subtlety of a hammer.

Oh fantastic, the man in front of me has very poor mat hygiene and is now in a position where I am directly facing the soles of his feet. The closeness is intimate. The smell is even more so. Namaste, my acquaintance. Namaste to your feet, specifically.

Of course the instructor has just told us to let go of all expectations, while expecting us to perform a sequence that took her fifteen years to master. The cognitive dissonance is, itself, a kind of meditation. I am becoming one with my failure.

Naturally, the class has now extended ten minutes past its scheduled end time, and the instructor is still speaking softly about gratitude and the breath, while I am lying in savasana plotting how to slip out without making eye contact. I have meetings. I have meetings.

Wonderful, the new yoga studio costs forty dollars per class and offers a class called Sweaty Bliss, which sounds less like a workout and more like a euphemism. The studio's marketing materials assure me I will transform. I will transform mostly by becoming poorer.

Oh good, the instructor is now adjusting my pose by physically pressing on my back, without asking. I did not consent to being adjusted. I am being adjusted nonetheless. Truly the personal touch I had been hoping for from a stranger in stretchy pants.

Brilliant, the class concludes with the instructor asking us to set an intention for the day. My intention is to get out of this studio and find coffee, but I have a feeling that is not the type of intention being requested. I shall lie. I shall set a more spiritual intention.

Oh wonderful, the renovation that was supposed to take three weeks has now entered its fourth month. The contractor has not been on site for nineteen days. The materials are sitting in my dining room. I have begun to consider my hammer collection a personality trait.

Of course the budget has now tripled, due to unexpected issues that the contractor describes as discoveries. We have discovered asbestos. We have discovered knob and tube wiring. We have discovered a small forgotten bathroom behind a wall. Each discovery costs eight thousand dollars.

Brilliant, the tile that took fourteen weeks to special order has arrived, and it is not the color I selected. It is, in fact, the opposite color. The supplier insists this is what I ordered. The order form clearly shows otherwise. The form is in my hand. Their copy, mysteriously, differs.

Wonderful, the contractor has just informed me that the original blueprint cannot be honored, because something he describes as load bearing prevents the open floor plan he previously assured me was possible. I shall now have walls. I shall always have walls. The dream has died.

Oh fantastic, the team has now finished demolition and disappeared. The kitchen is gone. The cabinets are stacked in the garage. The fridge is in the living room. They left a note saying they will return next week. That was three weeks ago. We have been eating cereal from the box.

Of course the new floors have been installed, and they squeak. Every step squeaks. The contractor assures me this will settle in time. The squeaking, he says, is character. I did not ask for character. I asked for floors. Floors that do not squeak when walked upon.

Naturally, the inspector has now flagged seventeen issues with the work that was completed by my licensed contractor. The contractor blames the inspector. The inspector blames the contractor. I, the homeowner, am caught in the middle and being asked to pay both.

Wonderful, the paint color I selected from a tiny chip in the store looks completely different on the actual wall. It is more orange. Significantly more orange. The chip claimed warm white. The wall is, in fact, traffic cone. I shall be repainting.

Oh good, the workers have now arrived at six in the morning, without warning, and are operating power tools directly outside my bedroom window. The note I left specifically requested no work before eight. The note, evidently, was decorative. I am awake. Wonderfully, terribly awake.

Brilliant, the project is finally finished, several months late and several thousand dollars over budget. The walk-through reveals that none of the outlets in the office work. The contractor explains this was not in the scope. I am sure all the other contractors I will need to hire to fix his work will be lovely.

Oh fantastic, the entertainer has not arrived, the cake has been knocked off the table by a child whose name no one knows, and the bouncy castle has developed a slow leak. Eleven six-year-olds are now sugar-frenzied and demanding entertainment. Truly the magical afternoon I had been envisioning for the last three weeks.

Of course one of the parents has dropped off their child two hours early, said see you at five, and driven away before I could explain that the party does not start for two hours. I am now a babysitter. I did not sign up for this. I shall add it to my resume.

Brilliant, a child has somehow climbed onto the roof of the playhouse and is now refusing to come down, citing the freedom of the high places. The other children are cheering. The parents are filming. I am the only one trying to fix the situation. I have become the villain.

Wonderful, the goody bags I painstakingly assembled with non-candy items, in respect of the host parents' wishes, have been declared boring by the children. They want candy. They want sugar. The carefully selected stickers and small notebooks are being thrown to the ground in disgust.
