Yes please, mom of player number twelve, please continue to videotape every play in landscape mode from behind the goal so that your child, who is currently picking dandelions in left field, will have a permanent record of the most pivotal moment of his career.

Brilliant idea by the team parent to start a group chat with thirty-two members and zero rules. I love receiving forty-eight notifications by ten in the morning, half of them about pickup times we already established last week, and the other half about who is bringing oranges.

What a delightful display of perspective when the dad of the goalie storms onto the field at halftime to explain to a coach with thirty years of experience how a youth U-eight defensive formation should actually work.

Oh wonderful, we're doing trophies for every kid again. Truly the foundation of a robust competitive ethos. I'm sure the children, all of whom received an identical participation medal, are absolutely thrilled and will remember this moment fondly the way I remember winning my first piano recital, which is to say, not at all.

Clearly the most important thing for an eight-year-old to learn from organized soccer is to fear disappointing the man on the sidelines who paid for his cleats, his travel team fees, his private skills coach, and his now-mandatory weekend tournaments out of state.

I love when the season-end pizza party turns into a parents' versus parents' philosophical debate about playing time and the children, who actually played the season, sit at a separate table eating in silence and clearly wondering when they can go home.

Wonderful, my password must contain one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one number, one symbol, one Klingon character, and the blood of a small woodland creature. And it cannot be any of the last twelve passwords I have used. Truly elegant security design.

Oh excellent, the website is forcing me to change my password again because it has been ninety days. I'm sure the resulting incremental variation, where I simply increase the trailing number by one, has dramatically improved the security posture of the global internet.

Naturally the security question is, what was the name of your first pet, a piece of information I have shared on Facebook approximately eight hundred times. Truly the impregnable fortress of identity verification.

Of course the two-factor code was texted to a phone number I haven't owned since two thousand seventeen. Brilliant. I shall simply click forgot password, which routes me to an email address whose password I have also forgotten, in a recursive loop of digital hell.

What a treat to discover that my password is incorrect, my email is incorrect, and according to the system, I have never had an account, even though I am literally looking at receipts from this very company in my inbox dated last month.

Yes please, send me a CAPTCHA where I have to identify all squares containing a traffic light, even the ones where one tiny corner of the pole appears in the lower right of an otherwise unrelated tile. I shall fail this test eleven times until the website takes pity on me.

Brilliant interface choice to disable copy-paste in the password field, ensuring that I must manually type a thirty-eight character random string of nonsense from my password manager, character by character, while watching it become asterisks I cannot verify.

I love that the two-factor authentication app has just decided, on its own, to log itself out of my account, and the only way to log back in is via the two-factor authentication app, which is currently logged out. Truly the chicken-and-egg problem for our times.

Oh fantastic, the bank now requires a biometric scan, a one-time code, my mother's maiden name, and a small DNA sample just to check my checking account balance. I'm sure this is preventing approximately zero fraud while inconveniencing approximately all of humanity.

Clearly the apex of modern user experience design is the moment when, after entering my password correctly, the site decides to send me a confirmation email I must click within thirty seconds, an email which arrives forty-five minutes later and routes me to an expired link.

Oh wonderful, Uncle Mike is back this year and immediately ready to share his political opinions, completely unsolicited, between bites of stuffing. Truly the gravy of family conversation. I have been counting the days since last November for exactly this moment.

Naturally my aunt brought her famous green bean casserole, which has been famous in our family for thirty years for being objectively the worst dish on the table. We all take a polite, small portion, push it around our plates, and tell her it was delicious. The tradition continues.

Yes please, grandma, ask me one more time when I'm going to get married, settle down, have children, and quit that job you've never understood. I love being interrogated about my life choices over yams, it really aids digestion.

Brilliant, the turkey is somehow both raw inside and burned outside, which I previously thought was a thermodynamic impossibility. My mother has discovered new physics in the oven, and we are all here to celebrate her contribution to science.

What a treat to learn that we are all going around the table saying what we are thankful for, and that the answers must be sincere, articulate, and emotionally resonant, and that we are starting with me, right now, with no warning.

Of course my cousin's new girlfriend, whom we are meeting for the first time, has dietary restrictions that no one informed the host about, and she is now staring sadly at a plate containing approximately one olive and a leaf of iceberg lettuce. Cool, cool, cool.

Wonderful, the kids' table has dissolved into open warfare over the last roll, while the adults' table is dissolving into a passive-aggressive conversation about who didn't show up to grandpa's birthday in March. Truly a feast of love and togetherness.

I love that we waited four hours for the turkey to cook only to spend twenty minutes actually eating, before everyone scatters into different rooms to watch football, nap, or pretend to be doing dishes while actually hiding in the basement scrolling on their phones.

Oh excellent, dad has decided this is the perfect moment to bring up the inheritance and the cabin and who is going to take care of the dog when they go on the cruise. Pass the cranberry sauce, please. I need something tart to match the conversation.

Clearly the spirit of Thanksgiving is best honored by my brother-in-law explaining, at length, the supply chain economics of mass turkey production while everyone else tries to enjoy their meal. Truly, gratitude is the theme, and we are all profoundly grateful that he eventually stopped talking.

Of course the appointment was at nine fifteen and I am being seen at ten forty-two. I love the system where I must arrive fifteen minutes early but the doctor may arrive eighty minutes late, and somehow I'm the one who feels bad about asking how much longer.

Wonderful, the magazines on this table were last refreshed during a different presidential administration. I cannot wait to flip through a Time Magazine speculating about who will win the next Super Bowl, eight years ago.

Truly inspired choice by the front desk to seat the waiting patients three feet from the check-in counter, so that everyone here can listen, in great detail, to a woman named Brenda discuss her sciatica with the receptionist for the next twenty minutes.

Naturally the television, mounted high in the corner, is playing a daytime medical drama in which a chiseled surgeon delivers shocking diagnoses to weeping patients. Very calming background ambiance for those of us about to receive results.

Yes please, do call my name now, then walk me into another room where I will wait an additional thirty-five minutes wearing a paper gown that closes in the back. This intermediate purgatory is truly the unsung architectural triumph of modern medicine.

Brilliant of the practice to require I fill out the exact same six-page intake form I filled out at my last visit four months ago, listing every medication, surgery, and family member's cause of death from three generations, because clearly none of that information was retained.

Oh fantastic, the man two seats down has started a phone call on speaker. We are now all part of his discussion with someone named Carl about transmission fluid. I had no idea I needed this education today, but here we are.

What a creative design philosophy, putting the children's clinic and the geriatric clinic in the same waiting area. Now a toddler is shrieking in a doorway and an eighty-year-old man is loudly questioning why anyone would bring a toddler to a doctor's office. Both are correct.

Clearly the most reassuring thing to do, when running an hour behind, is to put a sign at the front desk that says please notify staff if you have been waiting more than forty-five minutes, when staff are already deeply aware and unable to do anything about it.

I love how, after the entire morning of waiting, the doctor breezes in, asks one question, types for ninety seconds on the laptop, says we'll be in touch with results, and leaves. Truly worth taking the morning off work for. I shall do it again gladly in six months.

Oh excellent, we are doing trust falls in the conference room with people I have lawsuit-level disagreements with. Truly the optimal context in which to allow my coworker Greg to catch my entire body weight. I have full confidence in his commitment to my well-being.

Naturally the team-building exercise is a mandatory four-hour escape room experience on a Saturday, unpaid, with people I see forty hours a week and would gladly never see on a weekend. Truly the kind of bonding I have been craving.

What a delight, the facilitator wants us to share one thing nobody else in the room knows about us. I have, predictably, nothing to offer except that I'd really rather be anywhere else right now, including the dentist, including a meeting about quarterly reports.

Yes please, divide us into teams named after fruits and have us compete in a series of increasingly humiliating relay races involving balloons and spoons. I'm sure the synergy we develop today will pay enormous dividends in next week's spreadsheet review.

Of course the budget for the team-building day exceeds what any of us would receive as a year-end bonus. But it's the experience that counts. The experience of organized fun under fluorescent lighting, with a paid life coach, on a Wednesday.

Brilliant icebreaker question: if you could have dinner with any historical figure, who would it be. Susan answered Cleopatra, Mark answered Lincoln, and now it's my turn, and I'd really love to say nobody, I just want to eat alone, but I will of course say Ada Lovelace and pretend to mean it.

Wonderful, we are doing a personality assessment, and my profile color is yellow, which apparently means I am communicative and chaotic. Whereas my manager's profile color is blue, meaning analytical and reliable. I'm sure this will not be referenced in performance discussions for the next eight months.

I love the part where we are encouraged to be vulnerable and share our biggest professional regret, in a room with our direct reports, our managers, and one HR representative furiously taking notes. Truly a safe space, in the most legal sense of that phrase.

Oh fantastic, the cooking class team-building event has descended into a small kitchen fire, three cuts requiring band-aids, and one very passive-aggressive argument about whether onions should be diced or chopped. Nothing brings a team together like collective near-disaster.

Clearly the lasting takeaway from today will be the lessons in collaboration we learned while pretending to enjoy axe throwing with a CEO who has never met us before. I shall carry the memory in my heart and on Slack, where the photos will live forever.

Of course the company decided to remove all of the offices and replace them with one enormous shared room of long tables, because nothing fosters deep concentration like overhearing seven different conversations and one man clipping his nails at his desk.

Brilliant decision to put the engineering team next to sales, ensuring that one half of the room is trying to debug something while the other half is yelling into headsets about quarterly close. Truly an environment optimized for productivity.

Wonderful, we are now in an era where the only quiet space in the office is the disability stall in the third floor bathroom, and even there, you can hear someone on a personal call about their divorce. Truly the workplace of the future.

Yes please, install hot-desking on top of the open floor plan, so that every morning we can play musical chairs and then sit next to a new stranger whose lunch will smell strongly of fish at exactly twelve fifteen.

Naturally the only conference rooms left at three o'clock are the ones with broken videoconferencing equipment and a door that has been off its hinges since the spring. I shall conduct my one-on-one in the kitchen instead, surrounded by people heating up curry in the microwave.

What a treat to learn that the official solution to the open floor plan's noise problem is a pair of noise-cancelling headphones we are expected to purchase ourselves, then wear all day to drown out the very environment the company designed.

Oh wonderful, the new collaboration pod is just two beanbag chairs in the middle of a high-traffic walkway, with no walls, where people are apparently supposed to have casual, generative conversations while everyone else steps over their feet on the way to the printer.

Clearly the lighting choice of one continuous expanse of buzzing fluorescent panels overhead is doing wonders for my eye strain and my circadian rhythm. I cannot wait to go home at six and find that the sun has long since set without me ever noticing.

I love that the original sales pitch for the open floor plan was that it would foster spontaneous innovation and serendipitous collaboration. In practice, it has fostered Bluetooth headphones, Slack messages to the person sitting four feet away, and a profound craving to work from home permanently.

Truly an inspired choice to keep the only enclosed phone booth on this floor permanently occupied by a man who appears to be running a side business in cryptocurrency, judging by the volume and frequency of his calls.

Oh excellent, the weather app says zero percent chance of rain today. I shall now confidently walk three miles to the coffee shop without an umbrella, and naturally arrive completely soaked because the sky has decided to interpret zero as a suggestion rather than a guarantee.

Naturally the forecast for the entire week is sunny and seventy-two, except for the exact two-hour window of my outdoor wedding, which is now showing a thunderstorm symbol with an exclamation point. Truly the weather app has impeccable comedic timing.

Brilliant, the radar is showing clear skies while I am literally standing in horizontal rain. I love technology. I love when the satellite confidently insists that I am dry while my socks have become a marsh ecosystem.

Yes please, helpful pop-up notification, tell me at six thirty in the morning that there is a winter storm warning ending at five thirty in the morning. Truly a forecast for our times. Punctual, useful, exactly what I needed.

Of course the feels-like temperature is sixteen degrees colder than the actual temperature, which I suppose is the meteorological version of a participation trophy for winter. Yes app, I feel that it is cold, and I would feel even more strongly that it is cold if I had not, in fact, been told to expect that.

What a delight to discover that the heat index, which according to the app is one hundred and twelve degrees, was calculated based on data from three counties over. The lawn I am currently standing on is hotter than the surface of Mars, but the app maintains that it is merely warm.

I love when the ten-day forecast changes daily, recalibrating in real time, so that the day I had planned a picnic three days out has now reorganized itself from sunny to severe thunderstorms in approximately the last six hours. The future has never been more reliable.

Oh wonderful, the air quality index is one hundred and seventy-eight, but the app's accompanying chirpy little graphic shows a smiling sun and the message Looks like a great day to be outside. Yes, perfect, I shall now go jog through this acrid haze.

Clearly the app's confidence interval, displaying with three decimal places the precise probability of rain at seventy-three point eight four percent, is a profound and trustworthy estimate, and not at all the same vague guess that a man with a corkboard map made on television in the nineteen seventies.

Truly impressive how the hourly forecast shifts between sunny and storming approximately every fifteen minutes, leaving me to decide whether to commit to the umbrella, the sunglasses, or both, in case the universe decides to throw both at me in quick succession.

Oh excellent, the driver is twelve minutes away, then nine minutes away, then sixteen minutes away because he apparently decided to make a personal errand at a gas station before picking me up. I love watching the little car icon dance around the map like a confused beetle.

Naturally the driver is on a phone call on speakerphone in a language I do not speak, while taking turns at speeds that suggest he is either being chased or wishes to be. The five-star rating is going to be a real ethical dilemma at the end of this journey.

What a treat, the GPS has rerouted us through an industrial park behind a strip mall, despite a perfectly functional highway being available. I'm sure the algorithm knows something about traffic flow that the rest of human civilization has not yet figured out.

Of course surge pricing has activated, because it is raining slightly, and now the ride costs three times what it cost yesterday for the exact same trip. Pure dynamic market efficiency, truly the future of urban transportation.

Brilliant choice by the driver to crank the air conditioning to arctic levels, play an inspirational podcast at maximum volume, and ask me, with great enthusiasm, what I think the meaning of life is, all within thirty seconds of my entering the vehicle.

Yes please, drop me at the destination on the opposite side of the highway from where I actually need to be, then drive away while I cross six lanes of traffic on foot, dragging a suitcase. Truly door-to-door service.

I love when the driver cancels at the last second, after I've been waiting eight minutes, and the algorithm pairs me with a new driver fifteen minutes away. The system is working exactly as designed, by which I mean it is working only for the shareholders.

Oh wonderful, the vehicle is a luxury Tesla with a sticky floor, an unidentifiable smell, and three loose energy drink cans rolling around in the back seat. I shall enjoy my premium ride experience while gripping the door handle to avoid sliding.

Clearly the most pleasant detail of this ride is the moment when the driver realizes he doesn't know where the destination actually is, asks me for directions, then proceeds to ignore them in favor of his own intuition, which is, predictably, incorrect.

Oh excellent, the YouTube tutorial said this would take an hour. I am now six hours in, the wall has a new hole in it that wasn't part of the plan, and I appear to have purchased the wrong size of pipe wrench. Truly weekend warrior energy.

Naturally the instructions assume I already own a stud finder, a tile saw, a wet vac, a multimeter, and what they describe as a basic set of pneumatic tools. Just basic stuff every household keeps on hand, alongside the toaster and the can opener.

Brilliant, the IKEA cabinet came with three identical bags of screws, none of which are the size called for in step seven. I shall now spend forty-five minutes laying every screw out on the floor like a small archaeological dig, attempting to identify which is the M-six twenty.

Wonderful, the leak under the sink is now a flood under the sink, because the wrench I was using slipped and hit a pipe I did not previously know existed. Time to call the plumber I should have called four hours and one hundred and ninety dollars of supplies ago.

Of course the paint I picked, which looked like soft sage in the store, is now drying on the walls of my living room as a vivid radioactive lime. I shall claim it was intentional and call it a feature wall, and never admit otherwise.

Yes please, hardware store associate, ask me what project I'm working on, then look me up and down, smile thinly, and recommend I buy six tools I have never heard of. Truly looking forward to my ninth trip back here today.

I love when the YouTube guy says, and now you simply tap it into place, while gently nudging the panel with one hand, and three hours of brute force later I am still tapping it into place, with a sledgehammer, while the panel laughs at me from the floor.

What a treat to discover, halfway through removing the old tile, that there is a layer of asbestos beneath, and what was supposed to be a Saturday project is now a forty-eight hundred dollar abatement situation requiring a permit and a man in a hazmat suit.

Oh fantastic, the new floating shelf I just installed has fallen down with all my books on it, taking a substantial portion of the drywall with it. Truly a high-impact way to discover that the toggle bolts I used were rated for one-tenth the weight I asked of them.

Clearly the final touch of any DIY project is the moment when my partner walks into the room, surveys the destruction, and gently asks if I considered hiring a professional, which of course I did, and which of course I would have done if I were a normal, reasonable person.

Oh fantastic, the weather app confidently promised sunshine all day and now it's hailing sideways into my freshly washed car. Truly an outstanding feat of meteorological precision. I'm sure the algorithm will get it right tomorrow, after I've already cancelled the picnic and bought an umbrella I didn't need.
